entries.title: Chicago marca el cierre del Dinastía Tour de Peso Pluma y Tito Double P
entries.summary: <p>El público de Chicago sin duda le dio a los primos Peso Pluma y Tito Double P el cierre final del Dinastía Tour que merecían, con tres noches sold out en el United Center llenas de agradecimiento este pasado fin de semana.</p><p>Con alrededor de 30 fechas, Chicago marcó el final de su gira por Estados Unidos, donde les llevaron a sus fans su álbum en conjunto, DINASTÍA, lanzado la Navidad pasada. En el corazón del proyecto destacan el legado, el orgullo mexicano y, sobre todo, la familia.</p><p>Con luces brillantes y una pantalla mostrándole al público lo que pasaba detrás del escenario, la canción “All of the Lights” del rapero Kanye West alocó a todos porque, si algo quedó claro, es que los primos conocen bien a su público mexicoamericano de Chicago.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a60000" name="module-a60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“¿Quién quiere escuchar corridos esta noche?”, gritó Tito al micrófono mientras sonaba “Intro”, dando inicio a la noche.</p><p>Con referencias a la lucha libre en las visualizaciones y la promoción del tour, el diseño del escenario reflejó esa estética y le dio al público un acceso más cercano. El escenario contaba con escaleras en ambos lados que imitaban las esquinas de un ring de lucha libre, por donde Peso y Tito subían no solo para acercarse a los fans, sino también para reforzar la temática del show. Una segunda plataforma tambîen evocaba la forma de un cuadrilátero, terminando de transformar el escenario en una extensión del universo visual del Dinastía Tour.</p><p>Familias, jóvenes y seguidores fieles llenaron la arena, muchos vestidos de negro como parte de la identidad del tour. Cada letra fue cantada a todo volumen.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-0e0000" Field.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Proporcionada por Héctor Rodríguez</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>La noche comenzó con ambos compartiendo el escenario e interpretando temas como “7-3” y “billete” de su más reciente lanzamiento. Sus estilos encajan bien, con Peso adoptando un tono más áspero y pesado que recordaba a las características vocales de Tito.</p><p>Después, cada uno tomó su momento en solitario para interpretar algunos de sus mayores éxitos. Tito se apoderó del escenario con canciones como “EL LOKERON”, “NADIE” y “LINDA”, mientras que Peso puso a cantar al público con “QLONA” y “Lady Gaga”. Ambos se complementaban arriba del escenario, con rosarios iguales colgando de un lado a otro mientras corrían de punta a punta con una energía imparable, acompañados de bailarines e instrumentos en vivo.</p><p>La noche estaba perfectamente curada con invitados especiales como Julian Mercado, Armenta, e Ivan Cornejo, quien interpretó “RELOJ” con Peso, y un mini set de 21 Savage. Sí, 21 Savage salió al escenario e interpretó “redrum”, un momento de surrealismo mexicano perfecto que hacía mucho sentido.</p><p>Mucho de lo que caracteriza a Peso es su sonido distintivo, que mezcla los corridos tradicionales con flows y rimas que recuerdan al rap y al trap. Su apreciación e influencia de la cultura afroamericana se hace evidente al invitar a raperos como 21 Savage al escenario. En otras fechas del tour también subieron artistas como Boogie y Swae Lee.</p><p>Esa conexión se hizo aún más evidente en la forma en que el público respondió a la fusión de géneros, especialmente cuando las influencias del rap entraban en un setlist dominado por corridos, con temas como “AMG”. La colaboración de 2023 con Natanael Cano y <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/suenos-music-festival-chicago/2024/05/26/suenos-gabito-ballesteros-review-latino-music-festival-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>Gabito Ballesteros</u></a> sigue siendo un clásico que nos recuerda lo bien que Peso Pluma ha ayudado a difuminar las fronteras entre la música regional mexicana y los sonidos urbanos.</p><p>Como una de las ciudades con mayor población de la diáspora mexicana en Estados Unidos, esta parada se sintió profundamente simbólica. La primera presentación de Peso en Chicago no llegó <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/suenos-music-festival/2025/05/24/peso-pluma-returns-to-chicagos-suenos-festival-with-a-crowd-pleasing-set" target="_blank" >sino hasta 2025</a>, luego de que su set como cabeza del cartel en Sueños 2024 fuera <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2024/05/26/suenos-music-festival-peso-pluma-cancelled-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>cancelado</u></a> por condiciones climáticas, y otra aparición en el United Center también se viera cancelada por motivos de seguridad. </p><p>Sin embargo, desde entonces Chicago no le ha fallado: cada presentación en la ciudad ha sido un sold out.</p><p>Peso y Tito cerraron su tour con broche de oro. Sus fans fueron testigos de su vínculo en el escenario. No hubo nada más cercano o identificable que la amistad y el lazo entre ambos. Fue un asunto realmente familiar, una experiencia sumamente especial de presenciar que demostró que “la sangre no olvida su origen.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: White Sox reach .500 this late in season for first time since 2022
entries.summary: <p>It wasn’t THAT long ago that the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>’ record was at .500. It just feels like it.</p><p>The Sox were 2-2 to end March of 2025.</p><p>Then they lost eight in a row and finished April at 7-23.</p><p>But never mind that now. After beating the Royals 6-5 on Wednesday, the Sox are 21-21. They haven’t been at .500 this late in a season since they finished the 2022 season at 81-81.</p><p>So surely, the roar that emanated from the Sox’ clubhouse and could be heard down the hall was in celebration of this achievement in the team’s yearslong rebuild. Surely, that came up amid the hooting and hollering.</p><p>“No,” shortstop Colson Montgomery said. “We know we’re in a really good spot. We’re not really looking at the standings because there’s still a lot of baseball left. It’s definitely a good achievement that we can look at right now and see that things are going in the right direction.”</p><p>Maybe manager Will Venable, who has been pushing all the right buttons with this team, has a greater appreciation for the accomplishment, having played in the big leagues for nine years, many more than most players on the Sox’ youthful roster have.</p><p>“Yeah, for sure,” Venable said in his typical low-key demeanor. “Your record matters, and we want to keep going from here. Obviously, want to keep playing good baseball and just continue to stack good days, and the record will take care of itself.”</p><p>Maybe that roar wasn’t from the Sox’ clubhouse. The team’s business-like approach to their play belies the age of its biggest contributors. And on Wednesday, that was Montgomery, who went 3-for-4 with two runs and an RBI, including what turned out to be a much-needed solo homer leading off the seventh inning.</p><p>That’s because, after being staked to a 6-3 lead in the ninth, closer Seranthony Dominguez allowed a two-out, two-run homer to Royals star Bobby Witt. Dominguez recovered to fan pinch hitter Jac Caglianone to end it.</p><p>“That was a huge run to be able to tack on there,” Venable said. “Gave our bullpen a little bit of breathing room, made the difference in the game.”</p><p>“I did my scouting on the guy,” Montgomery said of reliever John Schreiber. “I do scouting on relievers before the game just because of a scenario where I’m leading off the inning and I won’t have much time to look at the guy. I knew where I needed to look and was committed to the fastball, and he threw it there.”</p><p>The top of the seventh also loomed large. Reliever Jordan Hicks entered and promptly hit No. 8 batter Isaac Collins and allowed a pinch-hit single to Carter Jensen. That spelled trouble with the Royals’ 1-2-3 hitters coming up.</p><p>But Hicks stuck out Maikel Garcia and Bobby Witt swinging and caught Lane Thomas looking.</p><p>“Really impressive,” Venable said. “Hicksy is feeling really good right now, he’s in a really good spot. There’s been some times where we used him in different spots. For him to come in in that leverage spot there was amazing.”</p><p>What wasn’t amazing was starter Noah Schultz’s control — again. He walked five in 4⅓ innings, allowing three runs and two hits and striking out five. But the way the Sox are going lately, they were able to overcome it.</p><p>“You can just see everyone is starting to be their true self,” Montgomery said, “and I feel like when you’re your true self, that’s when you’re most confident. I think confidence is infectious. entries.title: Will Venable: White Sox' enjoyment playing together making difference in results
entries.summary: <p>Outfielder Derek Hill played for five other major-league clubs before joining the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> in September. Though none of them finished above .500 in his time with them, his remark Tuesday about the Sox still was notable.</p><p>“This is the most fun I’ve ever had playing baseball. It’s incredible,” Hill said. “Every guy’s pulling from the same side. Whoever gets called up, traded over here, doesn’t matter.”</p><p>Hill said that after hitting a tiebreaking home run in the eighth inning and making a diving catch in the ninth, so maybe he was just caught up in the moment. Besides, many of the Sox’ players only know of losing with the organization, which has endured three consecutive 100-plus-loss seasons. How much fun could they possibly have?</p><p>But listening to others in the clubhouse, there might be something to Hill’s comments.</p><p>“I love my teammates here,” second baseman Chase Meidroth said. “We know what we’re playing for. It’s a lot more than for ourselves. We’re playing for each other. The energy is natural. It’s easy when you come to this locker room [because] you know you got this group of guys.”</p><p>Manager Will Venable thinks that’s one reason for the Sox’ revival, which had them within one game of .500 entering Wednesday for the third time this season. It also had them at 20 wins, which they didn’t reach last season until June 5 (20-43).</p><p>“I think that makes a very big difference,” Venable said of the players’ enjoyment playing with each other. “It helps these guys hold each other accountable, give each other energy every day and communicate well. We’re seeing it show up in everything that they do.</p><p>“It really started from day one, in everything that we do, it comes up that they believe in each other. Everything that we do in meetings on the field, we talk about games afterwards, I just get the sense that that connection is what’s making the difference.”</p><h3>AL Central parity</h3><p>The Sox entered Wednesday in second place, 1½ games behind the first-place Guardians, in a tightly packed American League Central. All five teams were separated by three games. Venable was asked whether he thought the division would stay so close.</p><p>“I have no idea. Teams go on runs,” he said. “You think about us and the fact that we’ve played five games against our divisional opponents, and it’s all against [the Royals]. So I really don’t have a good feel for the division outside just the records.</p><p>“We’ve got a long way to go. We’re excited no one has run off with it yet. We’ll just keep doing our thing.”</p><p>The Sox finally will face a division foe other than the Royals on May 25, when they open a seven-game homestand with the Twins and Tigers.</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>The game Wednesday was delayed in the fourth inning to treat a fan who had fallen into the Royals’ bullpen beyond the right-field wall. The fan was transported to a hospital for more treatment.</p><p>• Jen Pawol worked the plate, making her the first woman to call balls and strikes for an MLB game in Chicago.</p><p>• Catcher Kyle Teel went 1-for-4 with a run scored, a walk and a strikeout batting third as the designated hitter in his second injury rehab outing for Triple-A Charlotte. entries.title: Joliet man charged in fatal shooting of Kenwood maintenance man last month
entries.summary: <p>A Joliet man has been arrested in the fatal shooting of an apartment building maintenance worker in Kenwood last month, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Gaddis Price Jr., 38, is accused of first-degree murder and felony possession of a controlled substance, police said.</p><p>On April 2, police responded about 5:35 p.m. to a person shot at the building in the 4500 block of South Drexel Boulevard. Officers found Alonzo Johnson, 42, in the lobby, shot in his left hand, right shoulder and chest, according to a police report.</p><p>Officers spoke to a witness who said a building resident had argued with Johnson, then returned to the lobby and shot the maintenance worker, the report said.</p><p>Johnson, who lived in the same block as the apartment building, was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in serious condition. He died there at 8:06 p.m., according to the Cook County medical examiner’s office.</p><p>Price Jr. is expected in court Thursday.</p>

entries.title: Sky grind out ugly win against the Valkyries
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO— You won't win many basketball games shooting 36% from the field. But the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> found a way Wednesday night against the Valkyries, holding Golden State to 29.3% from the field and 26.9% from three.</p><p>That latter was a gift. The Valkyries, who had been shooting over 40% on 35 three-point attempts per game, went cold. But the Sky's defense deserves credit too. Their perimeter pressure improved from the Portland opener, helped by the return of veteran guard Natasha Cloud.</p><p>The offense went the opposite direction. The trio of Skylar Diggins, Kamilla Cardoso and Rickea Jackson, which had hummed a few nights earlier, struggled to score. Cardoso and Jackson finished the first half a combined 2 for 14. The Sky were 0 for 10 from deep and 4 for 10 from the free-throw line in the period.</p><p>Ugly stuff.</p><p>But the Sky held their own defensively, limiting the Valkyries to 28 first-half points.</p><p>"When things weren't working for us offensively, we stayed in it defensively, which is good," guard Jacy Sheldon said.</p><p>The second half didn't get much prettier for either team, but coach Tyler Marsh thought the Sky's effort improved. And the team got timely contributions when they needed them.</p><p>One key stretch came with just under three minutes left in the fourth quarter, with the Sky up 60-58. The Valkyries forced Jackson into picking up her dribble and it looked like a broken play. But rookie Gabriela Jaquez made a timely back cut, and Jackson found her for an easy layup. Next trip down, Jackson hit a 3-pointer, her first of the game. Then on the defensive end, Sheldon came up with a steal.</p><p>And that's how you grind one out on the road.</p><p>"This is the type of team that we've wanted," Marsh said. "We shouldn't take it for granted that when we play defense like this, when we have the effort that we came out with in the second half, we can overcome those offensive struggles. We just kept sticking with it."</p><p>Sheldon thought the 69-63 win displayed the team's budding identity.</p><p>"We got a lot of dogs," Sheldon said. "We got a lot of competitors, ultra-competitors. As far as our identity goes, you got a team full of people who are going to give it their all every game."</p>

entries.title: Cubs' losing streak reaches four after rare misplay by second baseman Nico Hoerner
entries.summary: <p>ATLANTA — Cubs second baseman <b>Nico Hoerner’s</b> knack for improvising plays that defy belief has a flip side, though it rarely is seen.</p><p>The ‘‘Oh, wow’’ gives way to an ‘‘Oh, no.’’</p><p>With the Cubs and Braves tied at a run apiece in the eighth inning Wednesday, Hoerner saw <b>Michael Harris II</b> sprinting down the line on a slow roller and decided his only chance to get him out was to shovel the ball underhanded with his glove to first baseman <b>Michael Busch</b>.</p><p>To the Cubs’ horror, the ball went over Busch’s head. Harris reached safely, and a night of what manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> called ‘‘awesome . . . wonderful’’ pitching by <b>Shota Imanaga</b> was about to go into a death spiral.</p><p>Imanaga departed, then reliever <b>Phil Maton</b> hung a couple of curveballs — one that pinch hitter <b>Mike Yastrzemski</b> hit for a tiebreaking double and another that <b>Mauricio Dubon</b> launched into the left-field seats for a two-run home run.</p><p>Braves 4, Cubs 1.</p><p><b>Raisel Iglesias</b>, who has yet to be scored on this season, finished off the Cubs in the ninth for his eighth save, and the Braves became the first team in the majors to reach 30 victories.</p><p>The Cubs, meanwhile, have their first four-game losing streak of 2026. In two days, the Braves’ bullpen has held them to two singles in 10 scoreless innings. The Cubs have scored a total of three runs during their skid.</p><p>‘‘We made a lot of really nice plays tonight,’’ Counsell said on a night leather was flashed on both sides. ‘‘I’m sure Nico — it was a tough play, not an easy play — I’m sure he would tell you, ‘I could have made that play,’ but it was a tough play.’’</p><p>Counsell knows his second baseman.</p><p>‘‘I think I made it a harder play than it needed to be,’’ Hoerner said. ‘‘Just kind of misread the timing of it. Looking back on the play, there was definitely time to transfer to my hand.</p><p>“But you do rely on instincts all the time, and I trust that works most of the time. . . . But it definitely stings to have an error lead to the game-winning run.’’</p><p>The official scorer gave Harris a hit, and Imanaga was saddled with the loss on a night in which he set the Braves down in order in five of his seven-plus innings, didn’t walk a batter and allowed only five hits, including a home run to <b>Drake Baldwin</b> in the fourth.</p><p>The homer came on an out-of-the-zone slider that Baldwin had to reach for, but he nonetheless was strong enough to hit it 402 feet over the center-field wall.</p><p>Wonderful pitching? Imanaga wouldn’t go that far.</p><p>‘‘My outing, if I didn’t give up any runs, the Cubs would have had a chance to win,’’ he said. ‘‘So I think when I’m looking at it, you know, I should have kept it to zero.’’</p><h3>Giving Liam a look</h3><p>The Cubs are taking a flier on reliever <b>Liam Hendriks</b>, who won the hearts of White Sox fans in two seasons as their All-Star closer (2021-22), then tugged on their heartstrings with his very public — and successful — battle against Stage 4 non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.</p><p>The Cubs signed Hendriks, 37, to a minor-league deal and initially plan to send him to their facility in Mesa, Arizona, with the expectation that he eventually will join Triple-A Iowa, Counsell said.</p><p>‘‘It’s essentially just depth right now and taking a shot at somebody who’s had a lot of success and see what happens,’’ Counsell said.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Fan hospitalized after falling into bullpen at Rate Field during White Sox, Royals game
entries.summary: <p>A fan was hospitalized after falling out of the stands and into a bullpen at Rate Field during the White Sox win against the Kansas City Royals Wednesday night.</p><p>The Chicago Sports Network, which was broadcasting the game Wednesday night, said on social media that a fan had fallen into the visiting team’s bullpen during the 4th inning and was taken to a nearby hospital. The incident caused a small delay during the fourth inning of the game.</p><p>“Hoping for a good recovery and health for the fan,” CHSN wrote on social media.</p><p>No information was available late Wednesday on the fan's condition.
